title: Prices Vote: Economic Conditions and the Incumbent
hook: Voters rarely audit a governing record line by line. They ask a cruder question — is life more affordable than it was? — and that question moves elections more reliably than most policy debates.
key_points: Retrospective voting is the pattern where people judge incumbents by recent conditions they personally feel, above all prices and jobs.
It makes governing parties partly hostage to forces they do not control, like global energy prices or supply shocks.
It also gives incumbents a strong incentive to visibly act on the most salient prices, whether or not the lever is large.
In September 2026, per NPR, the administration sought ways to bring down gas prices as an affordability debate loomed over the midterms.
Opposition parties adapt to the same logic: NPR reports Democrats centering affordability in a Pennsylvania swing district, reusing messaging Republicans ran in 2024.
The pattern predicts a role reversal after every change of power — whoever holds office inherits the blame for prices.
content_html: Political scientists have long noticed that voters behave less like auditors and more like customers. They do not weigh a governing record clause by clause; they ask whether things have gotten more or less affordable, and vote accordingly. That habit — retrospective voting — quietly shapes campaign strategy in every democracy that holds regular elections.
extra_html: The 2026 U.S. midterms show the mechanism from both directions. NPR's Franco Ordoñez reports the administration pulling out stops to mitigate high gas prices as an affordability crisis loomed over the election, and NPR's Steve Inskeep interviewed consultant Sarah Longwell on how cost of living was weighing on presidential approval. Meanwhile Tamara Keith reports that in a Pennsylvania swing district, affordability is the centerpiece of the Democratic message — a replay of messaging Republicans used in 2024, now aimed the other way. That symmetry is the point. Retrospective voting is not a partisan phenomenon but a structural one: it rewards and punishes whoever holds office when prices move, including for causes far outside a government's control, and it pushes incumbents toward visible action on whatever price voters notice most. Understanding it explains a lot of otherwise puzzling campaign behavior — including why the same argument changes hands every time power does.

related.title: Public Opinion & Polling
related.hook: What 'the people' think shapes what governments do — but measuring it is trickier than it looks, and a bad poll can mislead as easily as a good one informs.

related.title: Voter Turnout & Engagement
related.hook: Who shows up changes who wins. Turnout — the share of eligible people who actually vote — is one of the quiet forces shaping every election.

related.title: Why the Out-Party Runs on Corruption
related.hook: Democrats mentioned corruption six times as often in 2026 constituent emails as in 2022. That jump says less about new scandals than about what corruption does for a party with no power to legislate.

related.title: What Public Policy Is
related.hook: Passing a law is just the start. Public policy is the whole arc — from defining a problem to actually delivering a solution and seeing whether it worked.

flashcards.back_html: Judging incumbents by recent conditions you personally experience — prices, jobs, cost of living — rather than by a detailed assessment of their policies.

flashcards.prompt: Why does retrospective voting put governing parties in a difficult position?

choices.text: They are judged on conditions like global energy prices that they only partly control
It legally bars incumbents from campaigning on the economy
It means voters ignore the economy entirely

flashcards.explanation_html: Credit and blame attach to whoever holds office when prices move, even when the cause is external — which is why incumbents scramble for visible action on salient prices.

flashcards.prompt: What does the pattern predict about opposition messaging after a change of power?

choices.text: The affordability argument switches sides to whoever is now out of power
Affordability stops being a campaign issue for a full cycle
Both parties abandon economic messaging in midterms

flashcards.explanation_html: NPR describes Democrats in a Pennsylvania swing district running the cost-of-living argument Republicans used in 2024 — the same tool, new owner.
